title_es: Gestión de DNS con Cloud DNS
body_es: Cloud DNS es el servicio gestionado de Google Cloud para alojar zonas DNS con alta disponibilidad global. Una zona pública responde consultas desde cualquier punto de internet, mientras que una zona privada solo resuelve desde las VPCs que tú especifiques, útil para nombres internos que no deben salir de tu red. Cada zona agrupa registros de tipos estándar como `A` (IPv4), `AAAA` (IPv6), `CNAME` o `MX`, y DNSSEC firma esas respuestas para que un resolutor validador pueda detectar manipulaciones, aunque no cifra la consulta en sí. El reenvío de DNS, configurable de entrada y de salida, conecta la resolución de tu VPC con servidores on-premises en ambos sentidos, y el emparejamiento de zonas permite que una VPC resuelva registros alojados en otra. El TTL de cada registro, en segundos, indica a los resolutores cuánto tiempo pueden servir una respuesta cacheada antes de volver a preguntar a la zona autoritativa; bajarlo permite propagar cambios más rápido a costa de más consultas, aunque algunos resolutores lo ignoran y aplican su propio límite. Por ejemplo, un registro con TTL de 300 segundos sigue siendo válido en caché a los 120 segundos, pero a los 400 ya ha expirado y toca resolver de nuevo. Un error común es bajar el TTL a segundos justo antes de una migración y olvidar subirlo después: cada resolutor vuelve a consultar la zona autoritativa constantemente, multiplicando la carga y el coste por consultas sin ningún beneficio ya.
body_en: Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's managed service for hosting DNS zones with global high availability. A public zone answers queries from anywhere on the internet, while a private zone only resolves from the VPCs you specify, useful for internal names that must never leave your network. Each zone groups standard record types such as `A` (IPv4), `AAAA` (IPv6), `CNAME`, or `MX`, and DNSSEC signs those answers so a validating resolver can detect tampering, though it does not encrypt the query itself. DNS forwarding, configurable inbound and outbound, links your VPC's resolution to on-premises servers in both directions, and zone peering lets one VPC resolve records hosted in another. Each record's TTL, in seconds, tells resolvers how long they may serve a cached answer before asking the authoritative zone again; lowering it propagates changes faster at the cost of more queries, though some resolvers ignore it and apply their own cap instead. For example, a record with a 300-second TTL is still valid in cache at 120 seconds, but by 400 seconds it has expired and must be re-resolved. A common mistake is dropping the TTL to a few seconds right before a migration and forgetting to raise it back afterward: every resolver keeps hammering the authoritative zone, multiplying query load and cost long after there is any benefit to it.
example_code:
records = {
    "www.example.com.": {"type": "A", "value": "203.0.113.10", "ttl": 300},
    "api.example.com.": {"type": "A", "value": "203.0.113.20", "ttl": 60},
}


def is_cache_valid(ttl_seconds, seconds_since_lookup):
    return seconds_since_lookup < ttl_seconds


queries = [
    ("www.example.com.", 120),
    ("www.example.com.", 400),
    ("api.example.com.", 30),
    ("api.example.com.", 90),
]
for name, elapsed in queries:
    record = records[name]
    valid = is_cache_valid(record["ttl"], elapsed)
    action = "cache hit" if valid else "cache expired, re-query authoritative zone"
    print(f"{name} after {elapsed}s (ttl={record['ttl']}s): {action}")
example_output:
www.example.com. after 120s (ttl=300s): cache hit
www.example.com. after 400s (ttl=300s): cache expired, re-query authoritative zone
api.example.com. after 30s (ttl=60s): cache hit
api.example.com. after 90s (ttl=60s): cache expired, re-query authoritative zone
